nameStory: This beetle earned its "long-necked" name from its distinctively elongated neck region, which sets it apart from most other ground beetles. The scientific name "pensylvanica" means "from Pennsylvania," reflecting where early specimens were first collected and described by scientists.
description: The Long-necked Ground Beetle is a small but distinctive predatory beetle that prowls New England's open spaces. At only about a quarter-inch long (5.8-7.2mm), it's tiny enough to fit on your fingernail, but its proportionally long neck makes it unmistakable among ground beetles. Like all ground beetles, it's a fierce hunter that helps control pest insects, spending most of its time scurrying along the ground in search of prey. Its dark, shiny body gleams like a tiny armored tank as it navigates through grass and low vegetation.

idTips.label: Elongated neck
idTips.description: The most obvious feature - a noticeably stretched-out neck region between the head and body that looks almost giraffe-like for a beetle

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: Very small at just 5.8-7.2mm long - smaller than most ground beetles you'll encounter, about the size of a rice grain

idTips.label: Dark, glossy body
idTips.description: Shiny black or very dark brown coloration that reflects light like polished metal when you examine it closely

idTips.label: Ground-hugging behavior
idTips.description: Stays close to soil surface, running quickly in short bursts when disturbed rather than flying away

idTips.label: Open habitat preference
idTips.description: Found in sunny, open areas rather than deep forest - look in fields, meadows, and grasslands

habitat: Long-necked Ground Beetles prefer open, sunny habitats throughout New England, including grasslands, meadows, old fields, and prairie-like areas. They're often found in areas with sparse vegetation where they can easily move along the ground surface hunting for small prey. You're most likely to spot them in disturbed soils, field edges, and areas that get plenty of direct sunlight rather than shaded forest floors.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as soil warms, emerging to hunt in open areas. This is often the best time to spot them as they're actively searching for mates and prey.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most abundant and easiest to find. Look for them during warm days when they're actively hunting in grasslands and meadows.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall, though they become less common as temperatures drop. They may be preparing for winter by seeking shelter under rocks or debris.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in protected spots like under logs, rocks, or in leaf litter, remaining inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Despite being called a "ground" beetle, Long-necked Ground Beetles are actually excellent climbers and will scale grass stems and low plants to hunt for aphids and other small insects - their long neck gives them extra reach when grabbing prey from awkward angles!
confusionNotes: The elongated neck makes this species quite distinctive among New England ground beetles, so confusion is unlikely. If you see a tiny, dark beetle with a noticeably long neck in an open area, you've probably found your Long-necked Ground Beetle - most other small ground beetles have more proportional, compact body shapes.
compareHints: The Long-necked Ground Beetle is the only member of its genus (Colliuris) found in New England, making it unique in the region. Compared to other small ground beetles in the Carabidae family, its elongated neck region is the key distinguishing feature - most other ground beetles have more compact, proportional body shapes without the stretched-out connection between head and thorax.
